questions.q: What are the two forms of energy released during the process of combustion?
questions.a: The two forms of energy released are heat and light. A wrong answer here suggests the student is confusing physical changes (like melting) with chemical changes (combustion), or is guessing without recalling the energy output.

questions.q: If you cover a burning candle with a glass jar, the flame eventually goes out. Why does this happen?
questions.a: The flame goes out because the supply of oxygen, a requirement for combustion, is cut off. A wrong answer suggests the student does not understand that oxygen is a necessary reactant, not just an incidental part of the environment.

questions.q: A piece of wood is left in the sun, but it does not catch fire. Why?
questions.a: While the wood is a fuel and oxygen is present, the temperature of the wood has not reached the point required for combustion to start. A wrong answer shows the student ignores the "heat" requirement of the combustion triangle.

questions.q: Compare the burning of a candle to the melting of an ice cube; which one is a chemical change and why?
questions.a: Burning a candle is a chemical change because it creates new substances (carbon dioxide and water vapour) and releases energy. Melting ice is a physical change because it remains water. Confusing these shows a lack of understanding of the permanence of chemical changes.

questions.q: Is it possible to have combustion if you have plenty of fuel and oxygen, but no way to provide initial heat? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, combustion will not occur because the "heat" component of the combustion triangle is missing to trigger the reaction. A wrong answer indicates the student thinks combustion happens spontaneously without an ignition source.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that air is necessary for combustion.
questions.a: Place a candle on a plate and light it. Place a glass jar over it and observe the flame until it dies. A poor answer fails to include a control (like a candle burning openly) or fails to mention observing the change in flame status.
